items.readable_text:
Content:
The complete graph on [MATH: n] vertices, denoted by [MATH: K_n,] is the simple undirected graph on [MATH: n] vertices in which each pair of vertices is connected by an edge. That is, any two vertices in a complete graph are adjacent.

Content:
The complete graphs on [MATH: 1,2,3,4,] and [MATH: 5] vertices are shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/d661fcd6e3a1a440f3ef2787d713f3ec]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/b752414e707fbe2cdb7399fcc17e8b83]

Content:
Properties of the complete graph [MATH: K_n] :

Content:
- Each vertex has degree [MATH: n-1.]
- The complement graph is an empty graph (a graph with [MATH: n] isolated vertices).
- The total number of edges is [MATH: \dfrac{n(n-1)}{2}.]

Content:
To see why the last property is true, suppose we're counting the number of edges in a complete graph [MATH: K_n] with vertices [MATH: v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_n.]

Content:
- [MATH: v_1] is adjacent to [MATH: (n-1)] other vertices.
- [MATH: v_2] is adjacent to [MATH: (n-2)] other vertices (as well as [MATH: v_1] which we already counted).
- [MATH: v_3] is adjacent to [MATH: (n-3)] other vertices (as well as [MATH: v_1] and [MATH: v_2] which we already counted).
- [MATH: \quad \vdots]
- [MATH: v_{n-1}] is adjacent to [MATH: v_n] (as well as [MATH: v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_{n-2}] which we already counted).

Content:
Thus, the total number of edges is
[MATH: (n − 1) + (n − 2) + ⋯ + 2 + 1 = ∑_(i = 1)^(n − 1)i = (n(n − 1))/(2).]

Content:
A bipartite graph (or bigraph) is a graph [MATH: G=(V, E)] whose vertex set can be partitioned into two disjoint subsets [MATH: V_1] and [MATH: V_2] (i.e., [MATH: V_1 \cup V_2 = V] and [MATH: V_1 \cap V_2 = \emptyset]) such that each edge connects a vertex from [MATH: V_1] to a vertex from [MATH: V_2.]

Content:
Equivalently, in a bipartite graph, adjacent vertices always belong to different subsets [MATH: V_1] and [MATH: V_2.] As a result, bipartite graphs cannot contain odd-length cycles.

Content:
For example, consider the graph [MATH: G] shown below (on the left) and its partition (on the right), which demonstrates that it is bipartite.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/1d5715ece269b334e7ad7eb69a957334]

Content:
As you can see above, we have redrawn the graph [MATH: G] in a way that clearly shows there are no edges between vertices within the subset [MATH: V_1=\left\{v_1,v_3,v_5\right\}] or within the subset [MATH: V_2=\left\{v_2,v_4,v_6\right\}.]

Content:
In a complete bipartite graph, every vertex in the first set is connected to every vertex in the second set. A complete bipartite graph with [MATH: m=|V_1|] and [MATH: n=|V_2|] is denoted by [MATH: K_{m,n}.]

Content:
For example, the graph [MATH: G] above is not a complete bipartite graph because it is missing the edges [MATH: v_1-v_4] and [MATH: v_3 - v_6.] By adding these two edges, we obtain the complete bipartite graph [MATH: K_{3,3}] shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/6c2b15d729de29a01555307222ee06ed]

Content:
By the rule of product, since [MATH: |V_1| = m,] and [MATH: |V_2| = n,] we have that [MATH: K_{m,n}] has [MATH: mn] edges. For example, the graph [MATH: K_{3,3}] has [MATH: 3\times 3 = 9] edges.

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
The complete graph on [MATH: n] vertices, denoted by [MATH: K_n,] is the simple undirected graph on [MATH: n] vertices in which each pair of vertices is connected by an edge. That is, any two vertices in a complete graph are adjacent.

Content:
The complete graphs on [MATH: 1,2,3,4,] and [MATH: 5] vertices are shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/d661fcd6e3a1a440f3ef2787d713f3ec]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/b752414e707fbe2cdb7399fcc17e8b83]

Content:
Properties of the complete graph [MATH: K_n] :

Content:
- Each vertex has degree [MATH: n-1.]
- The complement graph is an empty graph (a graph with [MATH: n] isolated vertices).
- The total number of edges is [MATH: \dfrac{n(n-1)}{2}.]

Content:
To see why the last property is true, suppose we're counting the number of edges in a complete graph [MATH: K_n] with vertices [MATH: v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_n.]

Content:
- [MATH: v_1] is adjacent to [MATH: (n-1)] other vertices.
- [MATH: v_2] is adjacent to [MATH: (n-2)] other vertices (as well as [MATH: v_1] which we already counted).
- [MATH: v_3] is adjacent to [MATH: (n-3)] other vertices (as well as [MATH: v_1] and [MATH: v_2] which we already counted).
- [MATH: \quad \vdots]
- [MATH: v_{n-1}] is adjacent to [MATH: v_n] (as well as [MATH: v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_{n-2}] which we already counted).

Content:
Thus, the total number of edges is
[MATH: (n − 1) + (n − 2) + ⋯ + 2 + 1 = ∑_(i = 1)^(n − 1)i = (n(n − 1))/(2).]

Item 5 — Tutorial: Bipartite Graphs

Content:
A bipartite graph (or bigraph) is a graph [MATH: G=(V, E)] whose vertex set can be partitioned into two disjoint subsets [MATH: V_1] and [MATH: V_2] (i.e., [MATH: V_1 \cup V_2 = V] and [MATH: V_1 \cap V_2 = \emptyset]) such that each edge connects a vertex from [MATH: V_1] to a vertex from [MATH: V_2.]

Content:
Equivalently, in a bipartite graph, adjacent vertices always belong to different subsets [MATH: V_1] and [MATH: V_2.] As a result, bipartite graphs cannot contain odd-length cycles.

Content:
For example, consider the graph [MATH: G] shown below (on the left) and its partition (on the right), which demonstrates that it is bipartite.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/1d5715ece269b334e7ad7eb69a957334]

Content:
As you can see above, we have redrawn the graph [MATH: G] in a way that clearly shows there are no edges between vertices within the subset [MATH: V_1=\left\{v_1,v_3,v_5\right\}] or within the subset [MATH: V_2=\left\{v_2,v_4,v_6\right\}.]

Content:
In a complete bipartite graph, every vertex in the first set is connected to every vertex in the second set. A complete bipartite graph with [MATH: m=|V_1|] and [MATH: n=|V_2|] is denoted by [MATH: K_{m,n}.]

Content:
For example, the graph [MATH: G] above is not a complete bipartite graph because it is missing the edges [MATH: v_1-v_4] and [MATH: v_3 - v_6.] By adding these two edges, we obtain the complete bipartite graph [MATH: K_{3,3}] shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/6c2b15d729de29a01555307222ee06ed]

Content:
By the rule of product, since [MATH: |V_1| = m,] and [MATH: |V_2| = n,] we have that [MATH: K_{m,n}] has [MATH: mn] edges. For example, the graph [MATH: K_{3,3}] has [MATH: 3\times 3 = 9] edges.

---

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The complete bipartite graph [MATH: K_{m,n}] has [MATH: mn] edges.

Therefore, our graph [MATH: K_{5,6}] has
[MATH: mn = 5 \cdot 6 = \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}30}]
edges.
